title: Effect of Li 2 MoO 4  on Cold-Sintered CaTiO 3  Ceramic Composite: Densification Mechanism and Microwave Dielectric Properties

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: In recent years, the global community has been increasingly challenged by the urgent issue of energy shortages, alongside the gradual depletion of traditional fossil fuels. 7  In this situation, the development of low-energy manufacturing technologies has become essential for reducing energy consumption and promoting sustainable development. Although the fabrication of microwave ceramics and devices is highly advanced, sintering methods have been explored, such as conventional solid-state sintering (CSS), spark plasma sintering (SPS), microwave sintering (MS), flash sintering (FS), and two-step sintering (TSS). 8 ,  9 ,  10 ,  11 – 12  However, the processing routes significantly influence the microstructures, often resulting in grain coarsening, longer sintering times, higher cost and energy consumption, and substantial CO 2  emission. Thus, developing energy-efficient, low-temperature sintering approaches for fabricating high-performance microwave ceramics has become a significant technological challenge.

Recently, an innovative sintering approach for integrating microwave ceramic devices has been established. This method, called the cold sintering process (CSP), was first  proposed by the research group of Clive A. Randell in 2016, and is notable for its low sintering temperature. 13  This technique is particularly advantageous for its lower energy consumption, simple equipment requirements, and environmentally friendly densification mechanism. It enables high densification of ceramics (typically ~90% relative density) at a significantly reduced sintering temperature ( < 350°C), in a shorter time ( < 2 h) and under high pressure (50–700 MPa). 14  Under these conditions, the presence of transient solutions such as water, acids or alkalis, hydroxides, and inorganic salts leads to localized dissolution at particle contact. Initially, the ceramic material is uniformly moistened with a small amount of a transient solution, which partially dissolves the solid surfaces and forms highly concentrated ionic solutions at interparticle contacts. After that, applying pressure before heating facilitates particle sliding and rearrangement in the subsequent second stage. At the third step, the transient solution evaporates at elevated temperature and constant pressure, reaching a supersaturated state that accelerates molecular and ionic diffusion. In the final stage, the strong chemical potential gradient promotes dissolution-precipitation reaction, leading to effective densification through solid–liquid and solid–solid interactions. 15 ,  16 – 17  Overall, the CSP densification mechanism is facilitated by particle rearrangement and dissolution-precipitation, enabling efficient consolidation at low temperatures.

Since the first discovery of CaTiO 3  by Gustavus Rose, a German chemist, in 1839, materials with the ABX 3  structure have been called perovskites, a term that has driven the revolution in modern electronics. 18  In the ABX 3  type, the A-site is occupied by larger di- or trivalent cations such as alkaline or rare-earth metals, and the B-site is occupied by smaller cations, which are mainly transition-metal ions. 19  Within this crystal structure, A-site cations occupy dodecahedral sites, while B-site cations coordinate octahedrally with six oxygen atoms to form [BX 6 ] units where oxygen atoms occupy the face centers. 20  At temperatures above 723°C, the ABX 3  type forms a cubic phase. 21  These crystal structures provide great versatility, resulting in both electrical and physical features. The periodic table shows that 90% of its elements can function as cations in ABX 3  perovskites. 22  However, the structural stability is contingent on ionic radii (0.75 <  t  < 1.0), with the tolerance factor ( t ) = ( r A  +  r o )/( r B  +  r o ), where  r A  and  r B  denote the ionic radii of  A - and  B -site cations, and  r o  is the oxygen anion, respectively. 23  In fact, a  t  value smaller than 0.75 is characteristic of the hexagonal ilmenite structure, and for  t  > 1, a calcite-type structure will also occur, reducing lattice symmetry at lower temperatures. It has a unique perovskite structure that hosts a wide array of phenomena, including ferroelectricity, superconductivity, and piezoelectricity. 24  This structural versatility makes them highly attractive for advanced functional applications.

The goal of this work is to develop a CaTiO 3 -Li 2 MoO 4  ceramic composite using CSP techniques, a system that remains largely unexplored to date. In this work, CaTiO 3  is considered difficult to densify in CSP alone and often requires post-annealing treatment. To address this limitation, Li 2 MoO 4  was introduced at different weight percentages (5–25 wt.%) to facilitate densification at low temperature (< 250°C) and uniaxial pressure, revealing the underlying mechanism. The effect of the Li 2 MoO 4  weight percentage on x-ray diffraction (XRD), microstructure, Raman spectra, Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectra, and microwave dielectric behavior was systematically investigated. These findings provide a low-energy approach to fabricating high-performance ceramic composites, enabling broad-scale miniaturization of electronic devices in the future.

sections.heading: Material Preparation
paragraphs: Commercial CaTiO 3  powder (99.5% metal basis) with an average particle size of 2 μm was purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Company. The as-received CaTiO 3  powder was first calcined at 900°C for 3 h to completely remove impurities. The calcined powder was ball-milled in ethanol with a zirconium ball-to-powder mass ratio of 20:1 for 24 h, then dried overnight at 120°C. The dried CaTiO 3  powder was manually ground in an agate mortar and pestle, then sieved through a 200-mesh sieve. Li 2 MoO 4  powder (99.9% on a trace-metal basis) purchased from Sigma-Aldrich was calcined at 550°C for 3 h to remove organic impurities. The characterization and instrumentation details are presented in S1.

sections.heading: Cold Sintering Preparation of CaTiO 3 -Li 2 MoO 4  Ceramic Composite
paragraphs: To prepare the CaTiO 3 -Li 2 MoO 4  ceramic composite, the components were mixed to 5 wt.%, 10 wt.%, 15 wt.%, 20 wt.%, and 25 wt.% of Li 2 MoO 4  (corresponding to 6.3 vol.%, 12.6 vol.%, 18.6 vol.%, 24.5 vol.%, and 30.3 vol.%, respectively). Afterward, the powders were mixed and ball-milled in ethanol for 24 h as shown in Fig.  1 . Then, the slurry was dried at 80°C overnight. Subsequently, 1 g of CaTiO 3 -Li 2 MoO 4  ceramic composite was mixed with 15 wt.% deionized (DI) H 2 O as a transient solution and ground using an agate mortar and a pestle for 10 min. The moistened powders were loaded into a steel die (12.7 mm diameter) and uniaxially pressed under 350 MPa to form compacted green pellets. Initially, the preheating step was conducted at 80°C for 30 min to promote the homogeneous distribution of the Li 2 MoO 4  powder. Then, the cold sintering set temperature was increased from 80°C to 220°C and held for 1 h, with a heating and cooling rate of 5°C/min, using both a heater jacket and pressurized equipment under 350 MPa. After the sintering temperature was reached, the pressure was released, and the sample was cooled to room temperature. The CSP specimens were placed in a hot-air oven at 120°C for 12 h to prevent water absorption. Fig. 1 Schematic representation of the preparation of CaTiO 3  with different weight percentages of Li 2 MoO 4  as a composite and CSP parameters.

paragraphs: XRD analysis of commercial Li 2 MoO 4  powder identified a diffraction pattern that agrees well with the standard JCPDS card #00-012-0763 without any discernible presence of a secondary phase, as displayed in Fig.  2 d. The strong diffraction peaks are 12.3°, 17.1°, 19.8°, 21.1°, 21.4°, 23.4°, 24.8°, 26.5°, 27.4°, 30.5°, 31.9°, 33.1°, 34.3°, 35.4°, 36.6°, 37.6°, 38.2°, 39.5°, 41.5°, 42.8°, 43.6°, 44.7°, 45.3°, 45.5°, 47.4°, 48.4°, 48.9°, 49.6°, 52.4°, 53.1°, 54.6°, 54.7°, 55.1°, 56.3°, 57.6°, 59.1°, 61.3°, 63.5°, 65.3°, 67.2°, 68.7°, and 69.7°, corresponding to  hkl  planes (110), (021), (012), (211), (300), (202), (220), (122), (131), (113), (312), (410), (042), (303), (232), (223), (104), (241), (511), (422), (600), (152), (431), (520), (404), (342), (161), (324), (104), (054), (621), (315), (072), (262), (006), (116), (452), (713), (354), (182), (416), and (615), respectively. Also, the crystallographic data for Li 2 MoO 4  show rhombohedral symmetry with space group R-3(148), with lattice parameters a(Å) = b(Å) = 14.336 and c(Å) = 9.588. The ball-and-stick model of the Li 2 MoO 4  crystal structure, generated with VESTA, is shown in Fig.  2 e. It is a phenacite-type rhombohedral structure, which is formed by corner-sharing of large LiO 4  and small MoO 4  tetrahedra, and these atomic arrangements present a narrow open channel containing four- and six-member rings along the three-fold axis to provide sufficient space for cation and anion insertions. Two Li and one Mo tetrahedra share vertices comprising oxygen atoms, forming a three-dimensional framework. 41  Figure  2 f reveals the SEM image of the calcined Li 2 MoO 4  powder at 550°C for 3 h. It shows the irregular shape of a micrometer-sized Li 2 MoO 4  crystal due to its high density. It acts as a water-soluble solvent to facilitate mass transport, enhancing particle rearrangement and grain-boundary diffusion under high-pressure gradients. Figure S2a, b, c, and d shows the corresponding EDX and mapping images of the Li 2 MoO 4  in the presence of Mo and O atoms, excluding Li +  ions.

sections.heading: CSP of CaTiO 3 -Li 2 MoO 4  Ceramic Composite
Quantitative Phase Analysis and Density Measurement of CSP Specimens
paragraphs: The XRD patterns of the CaTiO 3 -Li 2 MoO 4  composite with different weight percentages of ceramics were isothermally held at 220°C for 1 h and 350 MPa, as displayed in Fig.  3 a. All sintered specimens exhibit the characteristic peaks of CaTiO 3  and Li 2 MoO 4  phases, consistent with the corresponding above-mentioned JCPDS cards. However, upon increasing the Li 2 MoO 4  content (5–25 wt.%), a secondary phase of CaMoO 4  (JCPDS card #01-085-0585) was detected. This secondary phase is attributed to chemical interactions between Ca 2+  ions from CaTiO 3  and MoO 4 2−  ions released from Li 2 MoO 4  during the CSP. In CSP, Li 2 MoO 4  partially dissolves in water, forming a transient ionic solution that releases MoO 4 2−  ions. While CaTiO 3  is generally stable, at particle interfaces the presence of the liquid phase facilitates limited migration of Ca 2+  ions into the solution. Subsequently, the strong ionic interactions between Ca 2+  and MoO 4 2−  species lead to the formation of the CaMoO 4  structure at the grain boundaries. 42 Fig. 3 (a) XRD of CaTiO 3 -Li 2 MoO 4  composites, (b) relative density of CaTiO 3 -Li 2 MoO 4  composite via CSP under 350 MPa at 220°C for 1 h, (c) photographs of CSP specimens with different weight percentages of Li 2 MoO 4 .

The relative densities of CaTiO 3 -Li 2 MoO 4  composite ceramics prepared by cold sintering conditions at 220°C for 1 h under a pressure of 350 MPa are presented in Fig.  3 b. As the Li 2 MoO 4  weight increases (5–25 wt.%), the relative density gradually increases to reach a maximum  ρ r  = 83.1–92.4% (Archimedes method, Eq.  1 ) and  ρ r  = 79.1–90% (geometric method, Eq.  2 ), 43  demonstrating that CSP can achieve a dense CaTiO 3 -Li 2 MoO 4  composite, and the calculated density values are listed in Table  SI . In this process, Li 2 MoO 4  plays a significant role as a transient liquid phase, owing to its relatively high solubility in water (79.5 g/100 mL at 20°C), 36  whereas CaTiO 3  is essentially insoluble. Upon dissolution, Li 2 MoO 4  is dissolved in water, which infiltrates the interparticle spaces of CaTiO 3 . During sintering, the solvent evaporates, and the solute precipitates at grain boundaries, effectively filling voids and enhancing densification via a dissolution-precipitation mechanism. Overall, the above results confirm the feasibility and effectiveness of Li 2 MoO 4  content as a transient liquid phase in CSP, yielding a high-density CaTiO 3 -Li 2 MoO 4  ceramic composite. Figure  3 c shows the photographs of CaTiO 3 -Li 2 MoO 4  composites with varying weight percentages (5–25 wt.%), and the specimens have a diameter of 12.7 mm and a thickness of 2–2.5 mm.

sections.heading: Structural Analysis of CaTiO 3 -Li 2 MoO 4  Specimens
paragraphs: SEM provides essential insights into ceramic processing by revealing particle distribution, pore connectivity, and the influences of additives on microstructure. In this study, the cross-sectional SEM images of CaTiO 3 -Li 2 MoO 4  composite (5–25 wt.%), sintered at 220°C under 350 MPa, are shown in Fig.  4 . Different magnifications of the microstructures consistently reveal smaller CaTiO 3  grains alongside larger Li 2 MoO 4  grains, highlighting the dual-phase nature of the composites. Figure  4 a and a′ shows the SEM image of 5 wt.% of Li 2 MoO 4 , where incomplete particle coalescence and limited necking indicate insufficient densification. As Li 2 MoO 4  increases (10–25 wt.%), the microstructures become more compact and uniform, reflecting improved particle rearrangement and densification, as displayed in Fig.  4 b, b′, c, c′, d, d′, e, and e′. Thus, the microstructure evolves into a heterogeneous, granular structure in which Li 2 MoO 4  particles infiltrate interstitial voids, promoting efficient packing and increasing relative density. Li 2 MoO 4  particles fill the spaces between CaTiO 3  grains, confirming that CSP enables dense ceramic consolidation at low temperature. These observations are consistent with previous studies using Li 2 MoO 4  particles in CSP. 44 ,  45 – 46  To further understand the dispersibility of Li 2 MoO 4  particles in the CaTiO 3  composite, EDX mapping and spectra of the Ca, Ti, Mo, and O elements were analyzed, showing that those phases are uniformly distributed as illustrated in Fig.  5 a, b, c, d, e, and f. Fig. 4 Fractured morphology of CaTiO 3 -Li 2 MoO 4  composites: (a, a′) 5 wt.%, (b, b′), 10 wt.%; (c, c′) 15 wt.%; (d, d′) 20 wt.%; and (e, e′) 25 wt.%. Fig. 5 (a) Fractured morphology of cold sintered CaTiO 3 -Li 2 MoO 4  composite (25 wt.%), (b–e) EDX mapping analysis, (f) EDX spectrum of CaTiO 3 -Li 2 MoO 4  composite in the presence of Ca, Ti, Mo, and O elements.

The polished surface of the SEM images in Fig.  6 a, b, c, d, and e reveals a dense and homogeneous microstructure with limited porosity while increasing the water-solubility of Li 2 MoO 4  content (5–25 wt.%). It indicates the effective densification during the cold sintering process, which is attributed to the dissolution of Li 2 MoO 4  in the transient solution followed by mass transport and reprecipitation at particle content under the combined effect of pressure and temperature. The elemental mapping images in Fig.  6 f, g, h, and i display a uniform distribution of Ca, Ti, O, and Mo throughout the microstructure, confirming the homogeneous dispersion of the Li 2 MoO 4  phase with the CaTiO 3  material. Figure  6 j shows an EDX spectrum, whose peaks confirm the coexistence of those phases. Overall, the dense, well-packed microstructure supports a satisfactory relative density and is suitable for fabricating microwave dielectric materials. Further, to confirm that we have analyzed transmission electron microscopy (TEM) studies of CaTiO 3 -Li 2 MoO 4  (25 wt.%). Figure  7 a, b, c, and d reveals different regions and magnifications of densely packed nanosized particles. During CSP, Li 2 MoO 4  partially dissolves in the transient solution and reprecipitates to promote interparticle bonding and pore elimination. The elemental mapping in Fig.  7 e, f, g, and h demonstrates a uniform dispersion of the Li 2 MoO 4  phase with strong absorption within the CaTiO 3  particles. The EDX spectrum in Fig.  7 i further verifies the presence of the constituent elements in those phases. Fig. 6 Sintered surface morphology of CaTiO 3 -Li 2 MoO 4  composites: (a) 5 wt.%; (b) 10 wt.%; (c) 15 wt.%; (d) 20 wt.%; and (e) 25 wt.%. (f–i) EDX elemental mapping image of CaTiO 3 -Li 2 MoO 4  (25 wt.%) specimens and (j) corresponding EDX spectrum image. Fig. 7 (a–d) TEM morphologies of CaTiO 3 -Li 2 MoO 4  composite (25 wt.%) at different magnifications, (e–h) corresponding EDX elemental mapping images, and (i) EDX spectrum.

sections.heading: Vibrational Characteristics of Sintered Specimens
paragraphs: The Raman bands in the range below 800 cm −1  are a mixture of internal modes, which refer to the vibrations inside the MoO 4  tetrahedron and movement of Li +  cations, and vibrations/translations of the [MoO 4 ] tetrahedron units are related to the external modes. 46  The bands above 800 cm −1  belong to the stretching ( v 1  and  v 3 ) of internal modes. 51  Based on the Raman spectroscopy of CaTiO 3 -Li 2 MoO 4  composite (5–25 wt.%), the overlap Raman active modes of those materials are listed in Table  I . The intensity of CaTiO 3  bands increases with the weight of Li 2 MoO 4 , and the Raman shifts of Li 2 MoO 4  (325, 823, 846, and 905 cm −1 ) are obtained in all CSP composites, displayed in Fig.  8 a. Also, we observe a strong peak at 877 cm −1 , which corresponds to the symmetric stretching of the [MoO 4 ] tetrahedron and is assigned to the CaMoO 4  phase formed by the chemical reaction. 52  The result indicates that the CaTiO 3 -Li 2 MoO 4  composite ceramics consist of a superposition and coexistence of these phases, as further confirmed. The FTIR characteristics of the CaTiO 3 -Li 2 MoO 4  composite (5–25 wt.%) were investigated, with emphasis on structural evolution, lattice distortion, and their implications for dielectric behavior. The wideband spectrum of CaTiO 3  showed a functional group at 400–4000 cm −1 , as shown in Fig. S4a. The peaks at 457 cm −1  are assigned to Ti–O stretching and Ti–O–Ti bridge stretching modes. 53  Also, the peak at 643 cm −1  belongs to the TiO 6  octahedral network. 54  The bands at 1618 cm −1  and 3387 cm −1  are assigned to the asymmetric vibrational modes of the hydroxy group (OH − ). 55  As shown in Fig. S4b, the characteristic peaks for Li 2 MoO 4  were observed at 471 cm −1  and 838 cm −1 , which are attributed to the Mo–O bending vibration mode and the stretching vibration of O–Mo–O in the MoO 4 2−  tetrahedron. 56 , 57  The IR spectrum of the CaTiO 3 -Li 2 MoO 4  composite is well matched with the corresponding peaks of CaTiO 3  and Li 2 MoO 4  phases, which suggests that Li 2 MoO 4  strongly adsorbs on the particle surface of CaTiO 3  and may form hydrogen bonds between the surfaces. This reveals that the peaks at 597, 694, 835, 1651, and 3347 cm −1  are observed in the ceramic composites, as shown in Fig.  8 b. All spectrum peaks are listed in Table  II , and suggest that dense CaTiO 3  ceramics exhibit better compatibility and a more uniform spatial distribution of the LiMoO 4  phase, thereby enabling successful cold sintering. sections.heading: Densification Mechanism of CaTiO 3 -Li 2 MoO 4  Composite by CSP
paragraphs: The densification mechanism of the CaTiO 3 -Li 2 MoO 4  composite during CSP can be described as a three-stage process, in which each step is interconnected and strongly influenced by the presence of a transient solution, and Li 2 MoO 4  is illustrated in Fig.  9 . In the first stage, the transient solution promotes local dissolution at particle surfaces, enhancing particle wetting and facilitating smooth packing and closer grain–grain contacts. In the second stage, under applied uniaxial pressure (350 MPa), the transient solution penetrates the interparticle voids. It acts as a lubricant, enabling particle sliding, rotation, and rearrangement, thereby resulting in initial powder compaction. During the third stage, the temperature is increased to 220°C under constant pressure. The elevated temperature enhances the dissolution of Li 2 MoO 4  within the transient solution at highly stressed particle contacts. The resulting differences in local solute concentration and chemical potential drive the mass transport of dissolved Li +  and MoO 4 2−  species through the liquid phase towards regions of lower chemical potential, such as interparticle pores and low-stress surfaces, where reprecipitation of Li 2 MoO 4  promotes pore filling and further enhances densification. 58 Fig. 9 Schematic diagram of the CSP mechanism of CaTiO 3 -Li 2 MoO 4  composite with DI H 2 O as a transient solution.

Although Li 2 MoO 4  has a relatively low melting point (701°C), 59  the processing temperature of 220°C is far below its melting temperature. Therefore, densification does not occur through partial melting. Instead, Li 2 MoO 4  partially dissolves in the transient solution and is subsequently reprecipitated upon solvent evaporation. As a result, the liquid phase becomes supersaturated with dissolved Li +  and MoO 4 2−  species, and reprecipitation occurs at particle contact and grain boundaries, leading to neck formation and a rigid, interconnected microstructure that enhances densification. Therefore, compared to traditional sintering, the CSP method offers a sustainable pathway to consolidate the CaTiO 3 -Li 2 MoO 4  composite through interrelated particle rearrangements and dissolution–precipitation mechanisms.

sections.heading: Microwave Characterizations of CaTiO 3 -Li 2 MoO 4  Composites by CSP
paragraphs: Lattice vibrational modes significantly influence tan  δ , and microstructural evaluation is important for microwave dielectric behavior. Figure  10 a shows that the tan  δ  of CaTiO 3 -Li 2 MoO 4  composites exhibits a gradual reduction from 0.0091 to 0.0017 (81% loss decrease) with increasing Li 2 MoO 4  content of the composites, which can be attributed to several interconnected phenomena. For example, pure Li 2 MoO 4  (tan  δ  ~ 0.0004) 36  is generally reported to exhibit a lower dielectric loss than pure CaTiO 3  (tan  δ  ~ 0.005). 62  Therefore, increasing the Li 2 MoO 4  content may reduce low dielectric losses. In addition, Li 2 MoO 4  suppresses space-charge polarization at grain boundaries, thereby minimizing Maxwell–Wagner-type relaxation that typically enhances dielectric loss. Li 2 MoO 4  promotes densification during CSP, reducing porosity and defect density, thereby reducing grain boundaries and scattering centers and enabling defect-induced relaxation pathways. Moreover, the presence of Li 2 MoO 4 , which stabilizes the composite microstructure and reduces the fraction of secondary phases or amorphous material that contribute to dielectric loss via mobile Li +  ions, enhances ionic conduction and the damping mechanism. Finally, the interfaces of CaTiO 3 -Li 2 MoO 4  composites are relatively benign compared to glass–ceramic boundaries, which exhibit less energy dissipation and Debye-type relaxation. Therefore, these intrinsic and extrinsic mechanisms elucidate the systematic decrease in tan  δ  with increasing Li 2 MoO 4 , the effectiveness of composition tuning, and the microstructural factors required to achieve low loss in microwave communication systems.

Q × f  increased monotonically from 466 to 3319 GHz as the Li 2 MoO 4  weight increased from 5 to 20 wt.%, and then decreased at 25 wt.% as displayed in Fig.  10 b. It reveals various factors, including (i) redistribution of Li +  ions localization at grain boundaries into a more stable configuration, residual ionic conduction pathway, (ii) Maxwell–Wagner polarization effect at heterogeneous phase boundaries, (iii) grain boundary scattering arising from high boundary density to introduce electromagnetic energy dissipation, and (iv) defect-induced polarization that is associated with compositional disorder and limits oxygen vacancy formation. As a result, the overall dielectric loss is reduced, leading to a significant enhancement in  Q × f  values. This improvement underscores the tuning of microstructural control to optimize microwave dielectric performance, particularly for applications requiring resonators and minimal energy dissipation in the GHz frequency range.
